plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks three waveform traces on a shared horizontal time axis to compare two ways of encoding a message on a radio carrier. The topmost trace is a smooth black curve with two broad crests separated by a single trough, labeled Signal at its right end; it is the slowly varying information waveform. Below it a red trace labeled AM oscillates far more rapidly, with the spacing between successive peaks held uniform while their height swells and shrinks: the excursion from peak to trough is largest beneath the two crests of the black curve and collapses to its smallest beneath the black trough, so the outline traced by the red peaks reproduces the shape of the signal above it. The lowest trace, drawn in blue and labeled FM, keeps a constant peak-to-trough height clear across the page while its cycles bunch tightly together below the signal crests and stretch apart below the signal trough. Setting the two carriers one beneath the other invites a direct comparison of which wave property carries the information, envelope height in one case and cycle spacing in the other. The drawing accompanies the treatment of the radio region of the electromagnetic spectrum, where amplitude modulation and frequency modulation are distinguished as the two schemes used to broadcast a signal.

interactionPlan.concept: A radio carrier wave can encode the same information either by varying its peak height (Amplitude Modulation) or by varying the spacing between its cycles (Frequency Modulation).
elements: Top trace: low-frequency information signal (black curve)
Middle trace: AM carrier wave (red curve, varying amplitude)
Bottom trace: FM carrier wave (blue curve, varying frequency)
Label 'Signal' next to top trace
Label 'AM' next to middle trace
Label 'FM' next to bottom trace
Vertical time-scanning marker line spanning all three traces
Dynamic readout on the marker showing 'Signal Height'
Dynamic readout on the marker showing 'AM Envelope Height'
Dynamic readout on the marker showing 'FM Cycle Spacing'
Overlay: AM envelope outline (dashed curve connecting red peaks)
Overlay: FM frequency decoder (dashed curve tracing frequency variation)

interactions.label: Scan time
interactions.teaches: Scanning across the waveforms shows that the AM wave's height directly mimics the original signal at every instant, while the FM wave's instantaneous cycle spacing does the same.

interactions.label: Decoding mode
interactions.teaches: A receiver extracts the original message by tracking the peaks of the AM envelope, or by measuring the changing density of the FM cycles.

demo_steps.title: The Information Signal
demo_steps.narration: The top black curve is the slowly varying message we want to broadcast. To transmit it, we must encode it onto a high-frequency carrier wave.

demo_steps.title: Amplitude Modulation (AM)
demo_steps.narration: In AM, the signal is encoded in the carrier's amplitude. Notice how tracing the peaks of the red wave (its envelope) perfectly reconstructs the original black signal.

demo_steps.title: Frequency Modulation (FM)
demo_steps.narration: In FM, the amplitude remains constant. Instead, the signal is encoded in the wave's frequency: the cycles compress tightly together when the signal is high, and stretch apart when the signal is low.

demo_steps.title: Scanning across time
demo_steps.narration: Move the time scanner to see how the instantaneous AM height and the instantaneous FM frequency both track the exact height of the original signal.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: AM hides the message in the changing height of the wave's peaks, while FM hides the exact same message in how squished or stretched the wave's cycles are.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Create three stacked line plots sharing an invisible x-axis (time), with distinct y-axes to prevent overlapping. Top plot: smooth, low-frequency black curve (e.g., 2 crests, 1 trough). Middle plot: high-frequency red wave whose amplitude is mathematically modulated by the top signal (envelope tracks the top curve). Bottom plot: high-frequency blue wave with constant amplitude but frequency mathematically modulated by the top signal (denser under crests, sparser under troughs). When 'Decode AM' is active, highlight the red trace and show a dashed envelope line. When 'Decode FM' is active, highlight the blue trace and show a dashed curve tracking its frequency. The timeScanner slider moves a vertical line across all three plots, updating readouts for amplitude and cycle spacing.

authoredContext:
Many valuable technologies operate in the radio (3 kHz-300 GHz) frequency region of the electromagnetic spectrum. At the low frequency (low energy, long wavelength) end of this region are AM (amplitude modulation) radio signals (540-2830 kHz) that can travel long distances. FM (frequency modulation) radio signals are used at higher frequencies (87.5-108.0 MHz). In AM radio, the information is transmitted by varying the amplitude of the wave (the figure). In FM radio, by contrast, the amplitude is constant and the instantaneous frequency varies.

This schematic depicts how amplitude modulation (AM) and frequency modulation (FM) can be used to transmit a radio wave.

This figure shows 3 wave diagrams. The first wave diagram is in black and shows two crests, indicates a consistent distance from peak to trough, and has one trough in its span across the page. The label, “Signal,” appears to the right. Just below this, a wave diagram is shown in red. The wave includes sixteen crests, but the distance from the peaks to troughs of consecutive waves varies moving across the page. The peak to trough distance is greatest in the region below the peaks of the black wave diagram, and the distance from peak to trough is similarly least below the trough of the black wave diagram. This red wave diagram is labeled, “A M.” The third wave diagram is shown in blue. The distance from peak to trough of consecutive waves is constant across the page, but the peaks and troughs are more closely packed in the region below the peaks of the black wave diagram at the top of the figure. The peaks and troughs are relatively widely spaced below the trough region of the black wave diagram. This blue wave diagram is labeled “F M.”

Other technologies also operate in the radio-wave portion of the electromagnetic spectrum. For example, 4G cellular telephone signals are approximately 880 MHz, while Global Positioning System (GPS) signals operate at 1.228 and 1.575 GHz, local area wireless technology (Wi-Fi) networks operate at 2.4 to 5 GHz, and highway toll sensors operate at 5.8 GHz. The frequencies associated with these applications are convenient because such waves tend not to be absorbed much by common building materials.

discrepancies: The generated signal spans 1.25 cycles and ends on a peak, whereas the source signal spans roughly 1.5 cycles and ends near the centerline after descending from the second peak.
The 'AM' and 'FM' text labels on the right are colored red and blue, whereas they are black in the source image.
A vertical scanner line with callouts is overlaid at x=0 by default, adding visual clutter to the start of the waveforms that is not present in the source.
evaluation.notes: The figure excellently implements the mathematical modulation of AM and FM with highly effective pedagogical interactions, though the base signal stops short at 1.25 cycles and the initial state is slightly cluttered by the scanner readouts.
action_items: Adjust the base Signal formula to span exactly 1.5 cycles (e.g. use `Math.sin(x * Math.PI / (10/3))` for x=0 to 10) so the curve descends from the second peak and ends near the centerline like the source.
Change the fillStyle for the 'AM' and 'FM' right-side labels in `pluginLabels` from their wave colors to '#222' (black) to match the source exactly.

Initialize `window.scannerPct = undefined` instead of `0` in the global scope and in the Step 1 state, so the scanner line and its callouts are hidden until the user moves the slider or reaches Step 4, preventing them from overlapping the start of the waves.
